concepts.name: Kotlin exceptions crossing into Swift and `@Throws`

questions.prompt:
```kotlin
suspend fun load() = coroutineScope {
  val a = async(start = CoroutineStart.LAZY) { fetchA() } // 1 s
  val b = async(start = CoroutineStart.LAZY) { fetchB() } // 1 s
  a.await() + b.await()
}
```
About how long does `load()` take?

choices.text: About 1 s: both `async` blocks start as soon as `coroutineScope` runs
It never returns: a lazy `async` only runs after an explicit `start()`
About 2 s: `await` starts each lazy coroutine, so they run one by one
About 1 s: the first `await` starts every lazy child of the same scope

questions.explanation: A lazy `async` doesn't start until `start()` or `await()` is called. Here `a.await()` starts `a` and waits for it, and only then does `b.await()` start `b`, so the calls run in sequence. To run them concurrently, call `a.start()` and `b.start()` first, or drop `LAZY`.

sources.title: Composing suspending functions
sources.claim: Code in coroutines is sequential by default; two `async` calls started before awaiting run concurrently; with `CoroutineStart.LAZY`, calling only `await` without `start` runs the coroutines sequentially because `await` starts the coroutine and waits for it.

questions.prompt: A ViewModel exposes `pager.flow.map { data -> data.map(::toUiItem) }`. The screen recollects it after a configuration change and also `combine`s it with a filter flow. What does adding `.cachedIn(viewModelScope)` at the end do?

choices.text: It writes the loaded pages to Room, so that they survive process death
It turns the flow into a `StateFlow` whose `value` is the latest list
It caches only the raw pages, so `toUiItem` runs again for each collector
It caches the loaded, mapped pages and shares one stream of PagingData

questions.explanation: By default a `PagingData` can only be used once. `cachedIn` multicasts the stream and caches the loaded data, including the results of transformations before it, in the given scope, so a recollection after rotation or a `combine` reuses what was loaded. It is an in-memory cache tied to the scope; persisting pages to a database is a `RemoteMediator`'s job.

sources.title: Load and display paged data
sources.claim: The `cachedIn` operator makes the PagingData stream shareable and caches the loaded data in the provided CoroutineScope; without it, PagingData cannot be recollected.

sources.title: Transform data streams
sources.claim: `cachedIn()` caches the results of any transformations that occur before it; by default each PagingData instance can be used once, and `cachedIn` multicasts the stream so later collections reuse the cached PagingData, which helps with operators like `combine`.

questions.prompt: Your shared KMP repository has `fun loadProfile(): Profile`, which throws `IOException` when offline. On iOS the app crashes instead of showing an error. Explain why, and how you would design the API so Swift can handle the failure.

model_answer.summary: A Kotlin exception that reaches Swift without being declared is unhandled and terminates the program. Declare the expected exceptions with `@Throws` so Swift sees a `throws` method, or catch them in Kotlin and return a result type instead.
key_points: Kotlin exceptions that reach Swift/Objective-C undeclared are treated as unhandled and terminate the program; a non-suspend function without `@Throws` propagates none
Annotate it with `@Throws(IOException::class)`: matching exceptions (and their subclasses) become `NSError`, and the function is a `throws` method in Swift
An exception of a class not listed in `@Throws` still terminates the app, so list what callers must handle or catch and map errors at the boundary
A `suspend` function without `@Throws` propagates only `CancellationException` to Swift

questions.explanation: Swift has no idea a Kotlin function can throw unless the signature says so, and Kotlin has no checked exceptions to tell it. `@Throws` is the contract: listed exceptions cross as `NSError`, anything else is still fatal. Many teams avoid the problem by returning a sealed result type from shared APIs.

sources.title: Interoperability with Swift/Objective-C
sources.claim: Kotlin exceptions reaching Swift/Objective-C that are not declared are unhandled and terminate the program; non-suspend functions without @Throws propagate none and suspend functions without @Throws propagate only CancellationException; exceptions of the @Throws classes (or subclasses) become NSError and such functions are `throws` methods in Swift; suspend functions always have an error parameter in the completion handler.

questions.prompt: Inside `coroutineScope`, a teammate writes `val user = async { api.user() }.await()` and then `val feed = async { api.feed() }.await()` (1 s each). Why does this gain nothing over two plain calls?

choices.text: Each `await()` returns before the next `async` has even been created
`async` always runs on the caller's thread, so the calls can't overlap
Both calls overlap, but the second `await` adds on the first one's time
An `async` without `CoroutineStart.LAZY` waits for `await` to begin

questions.explanation: Code in a coroutine is sequential by default. Here each `async` is awaited at once, so the first request finishes before the second `async` is even created: about 2 s in total. Concurrency comes from starting both `async` blocks first and awaiting afterwards.

questions.prompt: A ViewModel exposes `pager.flow.cachedIn(viewModelScope).map { data -> data.map(::toUiItem) }`. What is the problem with this order?

choices.text: `toUiItem` isn't cached: `cachedIn` caches only what comes before it
It crashes: `cachedIn` must come directly after `Pager.flow` and `map`
None: `cachedIn` caches every transformation in the chain, before or after
The mapped items are cached twice, which doubles the memory that's used

questions.explanation: `cachedIn()` caches the results of the transformations that happen before it. A `map` after it runs again on every collection, so a recollection after rotation redoes the mapping. Put `map` and `filter` first, then `cachedIn(viewModelScope)`, before exposing the flow to the UI.

sources.title: Transform data streams
sources.claim: `cachedIn()` caches the results of any transformations that occur before it; by default each PagingData instance can be used once, and `cachedIn` multicasts the stream so later collections reuse the cached PagingData, which helps with operators like `combine`.

questions.prompt: A shared `suspend fun sync()` has no `@Throws` annotation and throws `IOException`. Swift calls it with `try await sync()`. What happens?

choices.text: Swift's `catch` block receives the `IOException` as an `NSError`
The app terminates: only cancellation crosses without `@Throws`
The error is swallowed, and Swift's call simply returns normally
It doesn't compile, since only `@Throws` functions can be awaited

questions.explanation: Without `@Throws`, a `suspend` function propagates only `CancellationException` to Swift; any other exception that reaches Swift is unhandled and terminates the program. It does compile: a suspend function always has an error in its completion handler, so Swift can `try await` it. Add `@Throws(IOException::class)` to make the error catchable.
